paper_title: Online Mistake Detection in Instruction-Conditioned Procedural Video

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.

sections.content: An assistant monitoring person performing procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. Introduction Procedural mistake detection asks whether and how person performing multi-step task, such as cooking, assembling furniture, or following laboratory protocols, deviates from the prescribed procedure, as defined by its instructions. In computer vision, this is studied as videounderstanding problem: given egocentric video of person carrying out task, the system must recognize and temporally localize actions and determine whether they adhere to the procedures instructions [2, 9]. This capability could support an assistant that monitors person recording themselves while performing multi-step procedure, and notify them if mistake has been made while they can still correct it. To provide such feedback, model must interpret the video as it unfolds; since feedback delivered only after the task has failed may explain what went wrong but cannot help the person recover when the error occurred. This problem is challenging because visual appearance alone does not determine whether an action is correct. Pouring water into bowl is an ordinary action, but it is mistake if the instructions specify pouring the water into the bowl containing oats. The model must therefore relate visual evidence to the task instructions and distinguish between different deviations: omitting or adding step, performing an instructed step differently, failing to achieve its goal, or taking an action that repairs an earlier failure. These distinctions determine what went wrong and whether the procedure can still be completed successfully. Prior work has addressed parts of this problem in both offline and online settings. Offline methods use the complete recording to segment the video or align it with the procedures steps before evaluating the actions [6, 8, 9]. Instruction-conditioned approaches, including EgoOops [4] and ZeProM [11], compare observed actions directly with procedural text, but make their judgments after observing the entire recording. Online methods make decisions from the video observed so far. PREGO [2] detects deviations in action order, while ESTANet [10] also detects execution errors. However, these online methods do not assess actions against the explicit task instructions and do not provide the same combination of attempted-step identity, temporal boundaries, and fine-grained execution labels. This leaves gap between online monitoring and instruction-conditioned assessment: an online assistant needs to determine not only that an action is incorrect, but which instruction it attempted accepted: next window starts at the predicted end of the action (a) Modular approach = EXTRA: label ADDITION, skip verification Step Identifier which instruction was attempted? We address this gap by studying online, instructionconditioned mistake detection in egocentric video. At each decision, the system uses the video observed so far, the task description and instruction list, and its previous predictions. It identifies completed action attempt, localizes it in time, and classifies its execution as correct, modification, slip, correction, or an addition. Because an omitted step has no observed action interval, omissions are identified separately from the actions detected during the stream and after the entire video has been processed. We compare two prediction designs: modular approach that uses Step Identifier, Temporal Localizer, and Execution Verifier in sequence, and joint approach that predicts the same outputs in one response. Both maintain prediction history so that later actions, such as correction, can be interpreted in the context of earlier events. An illustration of both methodologies appears in Fig. 1. We evaluate our approaches on EgoPER [9], dataset of egocentric videos of five cooking tasks, with annotations for procedural steps and mistakes. Because the official training and validation sets contain only normal videos (without mistakes), we construct taskand error-stratified split that includes erroneous examples in training and validation, while retaining both normal and erroneous videos for testing. This enables us to study supervised, online mistake detection across the full evaluation set and separately on videos containing errors. Our results reveal distinction between recognizing the procedure and detecting its mistakes. The modular and joint approaches achieve similar temporal step-segmentation performance, but the joint approach attains higher error detection F1. modular component analysis helps explain this pattern: localization and execution classification perform well when their upstream predictions are correct, yet errors in those predictions can propagate through the pipeline. Predicting step identity, boundaries, and execution together reduces this dependency and improves end-to-end mistake detection. Thus, our findings suggest that the main benefit of the joint design lies in integrating decisions about whether an action is erroneous and how it relates to the instructions, rather than in improving temporal segmentation alone. In addition, both suggested approaches outperform the evaluated AEM and ESTANet checkpoints on the erroneous-video test subset, under our rigorous evaluation protocol. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on online and instruction-conditioned mistake detection. We then define the task and describe the modular and joint approaches. Next, we present the dataset split, evaluation metrics, and implementation details, followed by the main results and analyses of fine-grained mistake classification, temporal segmentation, and componentlevel performance. 2. Related Work Mistake detection in procedural videos is studied in two settings. Offline methods access the complete recording before evaluating an action, whereas online methods make decisions as the video unfolds, using only observations available so far [2, 10]. In the online setting, the literature also defines real-time mistake detection, which has strict requirement of instantaneous response. Since our work addresses online mistake detection, we focus our review on methods operating in this setting. We also review instructionconditioned methods, which assess observed actions against explicit procedural instructions. This perspective is central to our formulation: mistake is deviation from the provided instructions, rather than from the models general expectations about how the task should be performed. In this setting, the literature commonly separates procedural mistakes (omitted, added or reordered steps) from execution mistakes (a step performed with the wrong technique, tool, quantity or timing) [1, 4]. We use these terms to describe the types of mistakes recent work aims to detect. 2.1. Online Mistake Detection Existing approaches to online mistake detection differ in whether they detect deviations in the action sequence, errors in execution, or both. PREGO [2] detects procedural mistakes by comparing recognized actions with anticipated ones. Its recognition branch identifies ongoing actions, while its anticipation branch prompts large language model (LLM) with previously recognized actions and examples of correct sequences. mismatch between the recognized and anticipated step signals mistake. Because this comparison operates on step labels, an incorrectly executed action can escape detection if it is recognized as the expected step. PREGO also introduced Assembly101-O and Epic-Tent-O, adaptations of the original datasets [7, 12] in which test videos end at the first procedural error. These benchmarks therefore do not evaluate continued monitoring after mistake or recovery. More recent methods also examine execution quality. ESTANet [10] detects errors through inconsistencies among action predictions for the same video clip. Standard and error-sensitive detectors respond differently to execution errors, while detectors with different temporal contexts expose deviations from the intended action order. This allows ESTANet to detect both execution and procedural errors. However, it does not condition its decisions on instruction text, distinguish fine-grained mistake types such as slips and modifications, or explicitly associate an error with the instruction attempted and the required execution. Beyond detecting individual mistakes, PROVIA [13] emphasizes continued procedure tracking through errors and recoveries. Our work likewise maintains monitoring after recovery, however, we also ground predictions in explicit instructions and identify the attempted step and its execution class. This motivates our review of instructionconditioned methods, which assess actions against procedural text but have largely been studied in the offline setting. 2.2. Instruction-Conditioned Mistake Detection Offline mistake detectors use the complete video to segment the procedure into steps and evaluate each step using context from the full recording [6, 8, 9]. Among these, instruction-conditioned methods assess each step against textual instructions specifying how the procedure should be performed. This allows them to identify actions that appear reasonable in isolation but constitute mistakes because they violate an explicit requirement, such as using tape when the manual specifies glue. EgoOops is an example of this approach. Introduced by Haneji et al. [4], it pairs egocentric videos of five tasks with procedural text, temporal step alignments, mistake taxonomy, and justifications. Their detection method aligns the video with the instructions, then uses multilayer perceptron network (MLP) to classify each aligned clip as correct execution, mistake, or correction. More recently, vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled direct comparison between observed actions and instruction text. ZeProM [11] prompts single pre-trained VLM with the complete video and an ordered list of recipe steps, without additional training. The model segments the video, associates each segment with step, identifies errors with brief explanations, and lists omitted steps. Both methods assess instruction adherence after observing the complete recording, limiting their usefulness for timely intervention. Our models perform this task online, detecting mistakes while the procedure is underway and corrective action may still be possible. 3. Methodology Given procedural task description, its instructions in natural language, and an ongoing egocentric video stream of user performing the task, we propose detecting instruction deviations in an online manner by performing three steps: identifying completed instruction-step attempts, localizing them in time, and determining whether their execution follows the instructions correctly. We propose modular approach, which separates these decisions into three components, and joint approach, which predicts them in single response, and compare between the performance of the two approaches. 3.1. Problem Setting procedural task is specified by natural-language description and task dependent ordered list of Kd naturallanguage instructions = (i1, . . . , iK d). In this setting, the model observes an egocentric video incrementally, using only the available video and its earlier predictions. We distinguish an instruction from an attempt to perform it. An attempt corresponds to listed instruction even when its execution is incorrect. For example, pouring water into an empty bowl is still an attempt at the instruction to pour water into the bowl containing oats. completed attempt therefore means that the action has ended, rather than that its intended goal has been achieved. For each detected attempt, the system predicts step identity s, temporal boundaries [a, b], and an execution class c. The step identity {1, . . . , K} {EXTRA} associates the attempted action with listed instruction or identifies it as an additional action outside the procedure. The execution class takes one of the following labels: CORRECT The action follows the specified instruction. MODIFICATION The step is performed differently from the instruction, for example by stirring with knife instead of spoon or sweetening tea with sugar instead of honey. Such deviation does not necessarily change the outcome of the step. SLIP The execution fails to achieve the goal of the step and requires subsequent corrective action. Examples include pouring water into bowl other than the one containing oats. slip is labeled as such whether or not the person subsequently corrects it. CORRECTION The action mitigates the effect of an earlier slip, for example by transferring misplaced water into the bowl containing oats. This label describes recovery action rather than new mistake. ADDITION The person performs an unnecessary step outside the specified procedure, such as adding raisins when the original recipe does not include them. In this case, = EXTRA. The distinction between modification and addition depends on whether the action is an alternative execution of listed step or an extra step outside the procedure. For example, replacing honey with sugar while sweetening tea modifies an instructed step, whereas adding an unrequested ingredient as an extra action is considered an addition. In the case where no completed attempt is identified, the system returns NOT COMPLETED. This is not classification label, but an indication that the temporal boundaries of the window returned by the model need to be extended. Meanwhile, step omissions (c = OMISSION) are separate output, defined in Sec. 3.5, because they do not correspond to observed action intervals. To determine the temporal boundaries of actions, the video stream is processed continuously and sampled at one frame per second. The model applies procedure for incremental window construction defined next. 3.2. Incremental Video Processing Let τ denote the predicted end of the last attempted action (τ = 0 before any action has been predicted) and the end time of the constructed window. The model initially examines five second window starting at τ , i.e., [τ, = τ +5], as the potential window in which an action should be completed. If the model returns NOT COMPLETED, τ remains fixed and the endpoint, t, is extended by = 5 seconds, i.e., [τ, + ]. Thus, successive unsuccessful evaluations examine extending windows of 5, 10, 15 seconds, and so forth, all beginning at the same point. When an action is accepted and identified, its predicted boundaries [a, b] are expressed relative to the current window and satisfy 0 < τ . The corresponding absolute interval is [τ + a, τ + b]. The next window starts at the predicted action end and again has an initial duration of five seconds: τnext = τ + b, tnext = τnext + . All windows are clipped to the video duration. For example, if an action is detected in window covering seconds 015 and its predicted end is second 12, the next window covers seconds 1217. The system therefore resumes from the predicted action boundary, retaining any subsequent activity that appeared in the previous window. 3.3. Modular Approach As mentioned above, we propose two approaches for solving the problem of online mistake detection. The two approaches are illustrated in Fig. 1. The modular approach consists of the following modules: Step Identifier The step identifier receives the video in the current window [τ, t], the task description d, the complete instruction list I, and history of up to 12 previous eligible action predictions.1 It selects listed instruction, EXTRA, or NOT COMPLETED. Naturally, the model prefers the next step, but the identifier is not constrained to select instructions in their listed order. We formulate this problem as multi-class classification. Hence, the output is the highest logit value label, rather than freely generated response. If the prediction is NOT COMPLETED, the model extends the window and starts over (this can happen in every module). Otherwise, it passes the selected label to the Temporal Localizer. Temporal Localizer The temporal localizer receives the same video window and the selected instruction, or the EXTRA designation. It outputs the start (a) and end (b) 1This history length provides context for linking corrections to preceding slips while limiting the input length. times of the corresponding attempt, even if the action was performed incorrectly. The localizer can reject an incomplete attempt with NOT COMPLETED. rejection leaves the window start unchanged and causes the system to accumulate more video. For an accepted EXTRA action, processing ends at this component: the system assigns ADDITION and advances to the next window without invoking the execution verifier. Other localized attempts proceed to verification. Execution Verifier The execution verifier receives the localized crop [τ + a, τ + b], the selected instruction, definitions of the execution classes, and its previous execuIt classifies the attempt as CORRECT, tion predictions. MODIFICATION, SLIP, or CORRECTION, with textual explanation. If it rejects the crop as incomplete, the accumulation window is extended without advancing its start. The execution history provides context for interpreting the current action. In particular, correction may be recognizable only in relation to preceding slip that is no longer visible in the localized crop. This context is distinct from the history of step identities supplied to the step identifier. After verification, the system combines the predicted step identity, interval, and execution label into an accepted record, updates the relevant prediction histories, and resets the window according to Sec. 3.2. 3.4. Joint Approach The joint approach uses single adapted vision-language model to identify, localize, and classify an action in one response. It receives the accumulated video [τ, t], the task description d, the instruction list I, and history of up to 12 previous eligible action predictions. The output is either NOT COMPLETED or JSON record containing the step identity, start and end times, execution class, and textual explanation of the detected deviation, when applicable. As before, NOT COMPLETED response extends the current window by five seconds. An accepted record updates the prediction history and starts new fivesecond window at the predicted action end. Joint prediction may outperform the modular approach by avoiding error propagation between components. In the modular approach, an incorrect step identity affects localization and verification, while an inaccurate interval can remove evidence needed to classify the execution. The joint model predicts these outputs together, allowing their relationships to inform single decision. It still remains susceptible to errors propagated across time through its history and window updates. no observed temporal interval and is therefore handled separately from action classification. Let (cid:98)S be the set of instruction identities detected over the complete video. The predicted omission set is (cid:98)O = {1, . . . , Kd} (cid:98)S. This set is computed from the full detection record, rather than the bounded history used as model input. detected attempt counts as observed even if its execution is incorrect. During the procedure, the instruction order can indicate that an expected step has not yet been observed. Such an alert can only be provisional: step performed later is not considered omitted. We therefore finalize omissions only at the end of the video. 4. Experimental Setup Our experiments compare the modular and joint approaches under the same data split and video-processing procedure. We evaluate whether each model detects mistakes, identifies their types, associates them with the correct action intervals, and assess step recognition and omission detection. 4.1. Dataset and Evaluation Splits We conduct our experiments on EgoPER [9], which contains 389 egocentric videos of five cooking tasks: making coffee, oatmeal, pinwheels, quesadillas, and tea. 216 videos contain no mistakes and 173 contain mistakes or corrective actions. The dataset provides temporal step annotations for 4,741 segments: 4,237 correct executions, 215 modifications, 143 slips, 104 additions, and 42 corrections. The official training and validation sets contain only normal videos, while all erroneous videos belong to the test set. Since our supervised models require examples of mistakes during training, we repartition the videos into training, validation, and test sets, stratified by task and error class, without changing their annotations. Specifically, we move 148 of the 173 erroneous videos (approximately 85%) from the official test set into training and validation, retaining 25 erroneous videos for testing. Normal videos are also redistributed, with 183 assigned to training and validation and 33 to testing. The resulting partition appears in Tab. 1. Table 1. Baselines An omission occurs when one or more required steps are skipped, such as not checking the water temperature. It has Our main comparison is between the modular and joint approaches. For comparisons with existing mistake detectors, we evaluate released checkpoints of AEM [3], an offline mistake detection method, and ESTANet [10], an online method, on the shared 25-video test subset that contains mistakes, because the other 33 test videos may belong to the training or validation sets on which they were trained. Both baselines were trained on correct videos, whereas our models also receive annotated mistakes during training. These comparisons therefore measure performance under different supervision regimes. We evaluate AEM and ESTANet with our own evaluation code. For AEM, we use its default mistake probability threshold, τ = 0.5. For ESTANet, we group frames into segments by its predicted step label and mark segment as mistake when more than half of its frames are predicted as such. We also evaluate predictions using ESTANets released evaluator, which measures frame accuracy and segmental 1@10/25/50 (see supplementary). 4.3. Evaluation Metrics We report each metric as an unweighted mean across the five recipes. For binary evaluation, modifications, slips, additions, and corrections are grouped as errors, while correct executions are labeled normal. Corrections are included for scoring purposes, although they represent recovery rather than new mistakes. Error Detection Accuracy (EDA). The joint approach achieve slightly higher performance performance on both test sets: 93.6% vs. 92.1% F1@0.5, respectively, on all 58 videos, and 94.6% vs. 91.5% on the 25 erroneous videos. Their close performance suggests, despite their different prediction structures, the two approaches segment procedural steps comparably well. On the erroneous subset, both also produce segment counts close to the 280 annotated segments (283 for the modular approach and 284 for the joint approach), whereas AEM and ESTANet produce 368 and 387 segments, respectively. Their lower F1 scores (61.1% and 46.2%) are consistent with greater oversegmentation.2 Module-Level Performance Tab. 5 evaluates the Step Identifier, Temporal Localizer, and Execution Verifier both on all their calls and, where applicable, on calls for which the preceding component produced the correct output. For each window, the reference is the first annotated action that ends within it and has not already been assigned to an earlier prediction with IoU 0.5; if no such action exists, the reference is no step. The Step Identifier is scored on whether it identifies this reference correctly. The Temporal Localizer is scored on its ability to localize the reference action; its conditional scores include only calls where the Step Identifier named that action correctly. The Execution Verifier is scored on the label of the annotated segment with which its predicted span overlaps most. The conditional scores show how much each components performance depends on its input. The Temporal Localizers F1@0.5 rises from 85.0% to 96.9% on the full test set when the Step Identifier is correct, while its boundary error falls from 2.26 to 1.42 MAE in seconds. The Execution Verifier also improves with correct upstream outputs: macro F1 rises from 66.6% to 73.3%, driven largely by slip F1, which increases from 37.5% to 54.5%. Its CORRECT and MODIFICATION scores are already high, whereas CORRECTION remains more difficult, but also improves from 57.1% to 61.5%. The same pattern appears on the erroneous subset. Overall, localization and classification are strong once their inputs are correct, but upstream errors reduce end-to-end performance. 2ESTANet outputs frame-level labels, we aggregate consecutive frames with the same predicted step into segments for this comparison; we report the detector with the highest score. procedural tasks. First, training and testing on EgoPERs five cooking tasks does not establish generalization to other procedures or settings. Second, our split differs from the official split, and baseline comparisons are limited to 25 erroneous test videos due to data overlap. Moreover, differences in supervision and evaluation protocols prevent fully controlled comparison. Finally, replay-based online evaluation does not capture live interaction, alert usefulness, or error recovery, which remain future work. 6. Conclusion instructionWe propose two approaches for online, conditioned mistake detection in egocentric procedural video. The modular approach uses three components to identify steps, localize them, and assess their execution, while the joint approach performs all three tasks in single model. Both achieve strong temporal segmentation, and the joint approach detects mistakes more accurately, particularly slips. These findings demonstrate the potential of both approaches for detecting deviations as procedure unfolds and motivate evaluation on broader range of tasks and in online settings.

This is also demonstration of the output of each of the models that contain the instruction of the action, the time span, the classification, and the reasoning behind the classification. Figs. 2 and 4 compare the step segmentation and the mistake predictions of both our methods, AEM and ESTANet on two erroneous test videos from different tasks, pinwheels and tea. On step segmentation  (Fig. 4)  , the joint approach reaches segmental F1@0.5 of 85.7 on pinwheels and 88.9 on tea, the modular approach 78.3 and 88.9, AEM 64.0 and 76.2, and ESTANet 40.0 and 14.8. Both of our approaches mark the annotated off-script step in each video. On mistake detection  (Fig. 2)  , the binary F1@0.5, averaged over the error and the normal class, is 78.6 and 88.3 for the joint approach, 71.7 and 86.2 for the modular approach, 55.1 and 51.0 for AEM, and 23.8 and 9.5 for ESTANet. AEM and ESTANet give binary error decision, whereas our approaches also assign mistake type. On pinwheels, both of our approaches approaches detect the slip and the addition; the modification is split into two segments, neither of which reaches IoU 0.5, so it counts as missed. On tea, both of our approaches detect the modification and the addition; the joint approach also detect the slip. B. Implementation Details Shared setup. ESTANets evaluation protocol. ESTANet [10] does not predict segments. It labels each frame of the video as error or normal, and its evaluator scores this frame-byframe timeline. The timeline is split into runs of consecutive frames with the same label, and predicted runs are matched one to one with annotated runs of the same label at IoU thresholds of 0.1, 0.25 and 0.5 (F1@0.1, F1@0.25, F1@0.5).
